Replay

Starting a Replay game

Choose Timeline, Session, or Room to run the game, then connect its World to input and Godot scenes.

7 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Lifecycle callsChoose the ownerAuthor scenes around the WorldFirst runDefine replayable gameplayGodot frame loopInvitations and recoveryOwnership checklist

Store all mutable simulation state in an Odin World value. Replay retains its history and runs the game's rules offline or under a selected multiplayer policy. Device input, networking, Godot scenes, and persistence connect to that simulation through separate runtime owners. The game chooses authority and trust, prediction scope, and gameplay rules; Replay manages history, delivery, correction, and recovery under those choices.

Start with the Session starter for a small Godot project that runs offline or as a native host/client. Use Loot for engine-free gameplay, and the checked recipes for compact typed lifecycles. The Scrapyard authoring guide shows how those ideas grow into a complete editor-authored game.

Lifecycle calls#

Owner Setup Per frame or tick Read / submit Teardown
Local Timeline init advance current / read; emit inside a step destroy
Godot Session session_open session_frame Drain session_changes, read session_state; session_issue for actions session_close
Recoverable Room room_open room_frame Use room.session changes/state; submit with room_issue room_close

Session owns its clock, transport, and simulation runner. Room owns and drives its Session, so call the frame function of the outer owner rather than pumping both. Party manages enrollment separately: call party_frame, then use party_room_options to open Room after admission. Add Party for invitations and rejoin; local or direct Sessions can open without it.

Zero-initialize runtime owners, copy SESSION_OPTIONS for Session settings, and check setup errors before starting the frame loop. Keep an owner at a stable address until teardown. The shared conventions explain names, borrowed values and Godot exit cleanup.

Use import replaygd "godot:replay/godot" for those lifecycle owners. Optional scene, input, storage, transport and debug features have separate imports in the package map. Most Godot games add scenegd for their scenes and inputgd for device bindings. Debugging and low-level transport owners are opt-in; Session already drives its selected backend.

Choose the owner#

Game requirement Public owner/API Small runnable reference
Offline deterministic/value simulation Timeline, advance, revise_input Loot
Godot input, scenes and replay presentation Session or a local Timeline plus view adapters Hello
Listen host or dedicated authoritative server Session with Host/Server/Client/Observer roles Session starter
Co-op with invitations, reconnect and host migration Party → Room Cavecrawl
Cooperative live Godot body ownership owned plus Body2/Body3 and the authority runner Slopball
Competitive authority/prediction and historical queries net.Model policies through Session/Room Quickdraw, Claimball
Deterministic peer rollback P2P_Party + native P2P_Direct or RTC + p2p.Runner Duel

Use the existing example closest to your network policy. Their game-specific content is not required to use the library. Kit and its original games remain separate and independently runnable.

Hello's network scene deliberately builds the lower-level Enet/Delay/Server/Client loop directly. Use it when implementing a custom runner integration; the Session starter is the normal lifecycle example.

Checked API recipes instantiate the Session, Party→Room and admitted P2P→Runner lifecycle calls against the actual public API. They are checked natively and for WASM by the framework smoke command.

Author scenes around the World#

The Godot bridge provides typed views, definition baking, device/signal bindings, effect routes and body contracts. These owners keep node references and presentation lifetimes outside World while reusing its replay, action, journal and ownership protocols. Start with explicit typed callbacks; code generation is not required.

Run the focused bridge gate with nix develop --command bash tests/replay_bridge/run.sh. The performance assessment explains measured improvements, memory costs and why COW history was deferred.

First run#

From this repository, with its pinned development shell:

Shell
nix develop --command bash examples/replay_loot/run.sh
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_framework/run.sh

The first command executes a standalone world, corrects a contested transfer and checks a resumed timeline against a fresh run. The second is a bounded framework smoke command: it uses no account, public deployment or full-game parity campaign. It writes individual receipts and fails if any selected gate fails.

For an existing Odin/Godot project, make this repository available as the godot collection (-collection:godot=/absolute/path/odin_godot) and import packages such as "godot:replay", "godot:replay/net" and "godot:replay/godot". Godot scripts also use this repository's normal scriptgen/extension build pipeline. Core gameplay packages do not require Godot or generated scene bindings.

Define replayable gameplay#

Put mutable gameplay state in World: entity pools, RNG, inventories, cooldowns, ownership revisions and scheduled work. Use bounded value types and handles rather than pointers to nodes or another world's memory. Immutable authored data can live outside World, but it must be fixed and content-versioned while a session runs.

Write a step that mutates World using its input and Step.tick. Use emit for occurrences: recorded gameplay events whose identities let presentation match them across replay. Cross-entity actions are ordinary operations on that world. Do not read device state, wall time or live Godot transforms inside a replayed step, and do not play sounds or write files there.

Start with examples/replay_loot/main.odin for the complete local lifecycle. For authoritative networking, expose a net.Model with step/action callbacks, input and state validators, and held-input behavior. Hello's shared/hello/network.odin is a compact complete implementation. The model defines how scheduled controls and reliable actions affect the world; choose that distinction explicitly.

Godot frame loop#

Keep Session/Room and their models at stable addresses. Sample devices before the frame call; use the fixed-tick input helpers to retain short presses. For a direct Session, call session_frame, drain session_changes, then present a copied session_state. Check errors and drain all pending changes, not only one small buffer. session.control_consumed reports whether a simulation input step used the supplied control during that frame call. Clear pending button edges only when it is true; a frame that merely polls the network has not consumed them.

For Room, call room_frame and consume changes/state from room.session. room_issue submits actions and room_handoff requests a planned transfer. A fenced Room must keep pumping control/UI while gameplay waits. Do not make another authority by changing an epoch yourself. Room owns that transition.

Player identifiers and array indexes are different. Authoritative net seats start at 1; zero means no local player (for example a dedicated server or observer). P2P roster slots start at 0. Owner streams reserve owner 0 for no producer and map nonzero IDs through the application's authenticated roster. Convert a seat to an array index only after validating it; use the runner's documented identity mapping rather than treating a peer ID as an index.

Presentation journals report Begin/Update/Confirm/Cancel. Use their identity-aware one-shot/cue helpers so correction does not replay a sound or attach a death effect to a recycled entity. Remote interpolation and correction smoothing use copies; they must not change simulation values.

Invitations and recovery#

Party persists enrollment requests and grants before exposing them to the game. Open with a service/content ID, storage namespace, endpoint and invite policy; pump until recent selection is loaded; begin Create, Join or Rejoin. Use party_room_options once its grant is ready, then room_open.

A trusted co-op successor receives complete authority state. A competitive dedicated authority should fail over only to trusted infrastructure. Select those permissions intentionally; a network role name alone does not grant authority. See Party and dedicated rooms.

For deterministic P2P, P2P_Party registers the process and waits for the fixed roster. Native two-player games can use P2P_Direct; browser games use its RTC configuration. Bind runner slots only to admitted member identities. A fresh process needs both its stored enrollment and a compatible participant archive; the surviving runner keeps its history and rebinds the new authenticated generation. See P2P setup and native transport.

Use distinct native profile/database/archive paths for multiple local players. Same-origin browser tabs share a profile; use separate profiles for independent participants. Never put credentials or complete authority backups in invitation URLs. Plain enrollment WS is an explicit loopback development option; production configuration requires a verified confidential service connection.

Ownership checklist#

  • World/frame values are copied; live runtime owners are not. Keep Timeline, Session, Room, Party, Router and transport owners at stable addresses.
  • Keep model callbacks, immutable definitions and borrowed storage/cache owners alive until their users close. Schema owners may also borrow compiler metadata.
  • Close dependent gameplay transports/Room before Party and native stores. Destroy decoded checkpoints, recordings and schema owners on failure paths too.
  • Keep identity storage separate from gameplay archives. A checkpoint contains game/ledger state, not live connections or a transferable authority permit.
  • Persistent external side effects need an application/service idempotency design; a speculative gameplay occurrence is not an exactly-once external transaction.

Read compatibility before changing schemas or gameplay rules. Use the framework audit for actual test scopes and the remaining release assessment. Experimental support is not a claim that all engines, platforms, public networks or arbitrary physics are deterministic.
